prose: Geoffrey Litt shows that a genuinely useful personal AI assistant needs no fancy agent frameworks: his family's assistant, Stevens (named for the butler in 'Remains of the Day'), runs on one SQLite table of memories plus a handful of cron jobs for ingestion and updates, hosted on Val.town. The whole architecture is simple enough to copy and extend.

Every morning Stevens sends a formal, butler-style Telegram brief to Litt and his wife: the day's calendars, a weather preview, expected mail and packages, and tracked reminders. Beyond the daily brief they can talk to it on demand - forwarding an email, for instance, to have its contents remembered. The post's quiet point: memory plus scheduling, not agentic complexity, is what makes an assistant feel useful.
highlights: A family AI assistant built on a single SQLite memories table and cron jobs
Hosted on Val.town; deliberately simple enough to copy and extend
Sends a formal morning brief via Telegram: calendars, weather, mail, reminders
Supports on-demand chat, e.g. forwarding emails to be remembered
Named Stevens after the butler in Ishiguro's 'Remains of the Day'
Litt's point: memory + scheduling beat agentic buzzwords for personal tools
